name: Achiote (annatto) skin stain

lead:
Achiote, also called annatto or urucum, is the seed coating of the tropical American tree Bixa orellana. Its carotenoid pigments, mainly bixin, give an orange-red color, and Indigenous groups in the Americas have long used it for ritual and decorative body painting. Applied to skin, it leaves a warm orange-red stain.
For appearance, it works directly as a tint or paint on skin, and traditionally on hair, as with the Tsáchila men of Ecuador. It has also been described historically as a sunscreen and insect repellent, though those uses have not been established.

paras: Traditionally the seeds are crushed or the pigment is mixed with oil or water into a paste and applied to skin or hair. Modern cosmetic products use annatto extract as a colorant. Color deepens or fades depending on the form used.

Annatto is considered safe for most people in food amounts, but rare allergic reactions such as hives and possibly anaphylaxis have been reported. Skin staining can persist for days, and sun protection claims are not established.

lead: Achiote, known as annatto in English and urucum in Brazil, is an orange-red colorant made from the seeds of Bixa orellana, a tree native to tropical regions of the Americas.[1] The pigments sit in the waxy coating of the seeds; bixin is fat-soluble and makes up roughly 70 to 80 percent of the pigment, while norbixin is the water-soluble form.[1]

Its appearance use is as a skin and hair stain. The page on annatto notes that the plant was probably first used for non-food purposes including ritual and decorative body painting, sunscreen, insect repellent and medicine, that body painting remains important among some Brazilian Indigenous groups such as the Wari', and that Tsáchila men of Ecuador traditionally dye their hair bright orange with crushed seeds.[1]

paras: The seeds contain about 4.5 to 5.5 percent pigment. A higher bixin share gives a more orange tone, and norbixin gives a more yellow one. Unlike beta-carotene, these pigments are not precursors of vitamin A.[1]

Body painting with annatto is described as ritual and decorative among Indigenous groups of the Americas, and it continues among some groups in Brazil.[1] Tsáchila men dye their hair orange with crushed seeds.[1]

A 2025 review summarized by Wikipedia found annatto safe for most people at typical food amounts, with rare allergic reactions such as hives and possibly anaphylaxis.[1] In the US it is a color additive exempt from certification; in the EU it is E160b.[1]
